**We built an AI agent with an AI coding assistant. Here's what broke.**

Concept Buddy is our new onboarding assistant — it answers new joiners' small questions and updates a live dashboard as they go, pulling answers straight from company systems instead of guessing.

We built it with Claude Code, no upfront design doc — just prompt, build, review, repeat.

What surprised us wasn't whether an AI assistant could build working software. It's that "working" wasn't the bar. Tests passed, features ran, and it was still often wrong in ways only a human catches: documentation the model never saw, patches instead of fixes, one agent's judgment call standing in for a rule that belonged in code.

The pattern that helped most: Explore, Plan, **Question** (ask why the alternatives were rejected), then Verify. Question was the cheapest step and the one that caught the most.

Full writeup — two parts, one on working with the assistant, one on what it built: [link]

**We built an AI agent with an AI coding assistant. Here's the one mistake that taught me the most.**

We started simple: one agent, one instruction, for Concept Buddy — our new onboarding assistant at Concept Reply. As steps piled on, the instruction grew until the agent lost track of where the user even was.

So I did what every team does: split it into specialists. Seven agents — five onboarding steps, one for Q&A, one orchestrator to route between them.

It made things worse. The orchestrator was just another model making a judgment call, on every message, about who should answer — and that call wasn't reliable either.

We collapsed it back to one agent, two skills, and explicit state tracking progress. That held.

The lesson: another agent isn't a structural win by default. Reach for one only when the task needs its own context window, real concurrency, or a different trust boundary. Otherwise you've just added a second thing that has to be right.
